chunks: "Sure. I'll draw the master on the left, say a microcontroller, and two horizontal lines coming out of it: SCL on top and SDA below.
Every slave hangs off those two lines in parallel: SCL goes to SCL, SDA goes to SDA, no crossing like you'd do for UART.
Then at the far end of the bus I put one resistor from each line up to the supply, typically around 2. 2 to 4. 7 kilohms at 3.
3 volts, so that's my pull-ups, one per line for the whole bus, not one per device. Then I add the stuff people forget. All the grounds tie together.
Each chip has its own VDD pin with a 100 nanofarads decoupling capacitor, and the pull-ups go to the same rail the I2C pins are powered from.
Slaves with address pins get A0, A1 and A2 strapped high or low so no two share an address.
If a slave has an interrupt or alert pin, that's a separate wire back to an MCU GPIO, not part of the bus.

I'd also say what's happening electrically: every driver is an open-drain transistor that can only pull the line to ground, and the resistors pull it high when nobody's talking, which is why any number of devices can share the wire without fighting."
